title: Interval names and quality
description: Memorize interval number vs quality, the half-step table, and one-string fret offsets.

cards.front: What is an interval, and what two parts does its name have?
cards.back: The distance between two notes. Number (size) from inclusive letter count, then quality from how wide that numbered interval is in half steps.

cards.front: How do you find an interval’s number?
cards.back: Count letter names inclusively from the lower note to the upper. C to E is a 3rd (C D E). C to G is a 5th. The same note twice is a 1st (unison). C to the next C is an 8th (octave).

cards.front: What are the five interval qualities?
Which interval numbers can be perfect? Which can be major or minor?
cards.back: Perfect: unisons, 4ths, 5ths, and octaves. Major and minor: 2nds, 3rds, 6ths, and 7ths.

cards.front: How are augmented and diminished defined from perfect, major, and minor?
cards.back: Augmented is one half step wider than perfect or major. Diminished is one half step narrower than perfect or minor.

cards.front: How many half steps are P1, m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, and P5?
cards.back: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7. The missing 6 is the tritone (A4 / d5).

cards.front: How many half steps are A4/d5, m6, M6, m7, M7, and P8?
Name the note a m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, A4, d5, and P5 above C.
cards.back: D♭, D, E♭, E, F, F♯, G♭, G.

cards.front: Name the note a m6, M6, m7, M7, and P8 above C.
cards.back: A♭, A, B♭, B, and C.

cards.front: What is the reference for deciding quality?
cards.back: The major scale built on the lower note. If the upper note is in that scale, 2nds, 3rds, 6ths, and 7ths are major; 4ths, 5ths, and octaves are perfect.

cards.front: What happens when you lower or raise a major, minor, or perfect interval by a half step?
cards.back: Major down → minor. Minor down → diminished. Major up → augmented. Perfect down → diminished; perfect up → augmented. A diminished 7th is two half steps below the major 7th.

cards.front: Are half-step counts the definition of an interval name?
cards.back: No. They are a check. Count letters first, then use half steps for quality. C to D♯ (A2) and C to E♭ (m3) are both 3 half steps but different names and functions.

cards.front: Why is C to D♯ not a minor 3rd even though it is 3 half steps?
cards.back: The letters span C–D, a 2nd, so it is an augmented 2nd. A minor 3rd must use the letter E (C D E).

cards.front: What two interval names share the tritone size?
cards.back: Augmented 4th (C to F♯) and diminished 5th (C to G♭). Both are 6 half steps. They sound identical on guitar; spelling depends on context. “Tritone” names the size, not a substitute for the proper name.

cards.front: What interval pair makes a major triad? A minor triad?
cards.back: Major: root + major 3rd + perfect 5th. Minor: root + minor 3rd + perfect 5th. The 3rd’s quality is what changes.

cards.front: What 7th does a major 7th chord add? A dominant 7th?
cards.back: A major 7th chord adds a major 7th. A dominant 7th adds a minor 7th.

cards.front: On one string, what fret offsets from the lower note are m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, tritone, P5, m6, M6, m7, M7, P8?
From G on string 6 fret 3, name fret 7, fret 6, fret 10, and fret 9 as intervals above G.
cards.back: Fret 7 is B, M3 (+4). Fret 6 is B♭, m3 (+3). Fret 10 is D, P5 (+7). Fret 9 is C♯, A4 (letters G A B C); the same fret is also D♭, a d5.

cards.front: Name each interval by letters and quality: C to E♭, C to G, D to F♯, D to C, A to E♭.
Give the half-step count for P4, M6, m7, M2, and P5.
From C on string 5 fret 3, name the notes and intervals at frets 7, 8, and 10.
